title: Inferences
lead: Inference questions give you an unfinished passage about a subject you have probably never met and ask “Which choice most logically completes the text?” They are often the hardest Reading and Writing questions, because the answer is not written down anywhere. There is a specific, learnable logic to them.

parts.title: Part 1 · An argument with a gap
parts.html:
Every inference passage is a small argument, and an argument has two kinds of parts:

  • Premises: the facts the argument is built on.
  • The conclusion: the claim those facts are meant to support.

The blank is the piece that is missing. Sometimes it is the conclusion. Sometimes the conclusion is already stated and the blank is the missing link that explains it. The word just before the blank tells you which:

Before the blankThe blank is
“This suggests that…”, “Therefore…”, “These results imply…”The conclusion
“…because…”, “This is since…”A reason or link that supports a conclusion already given
“However…”, “…though…”A qualification or limit

If premises and conclusions feel too formal, think of the sentences as clues and the blank as what the clues add up to. Either way the task is the same: find what the argument is missing and fill the gap.

An inference on the SAT is not a guess and not a creative reading. It is a small logical step that the text forces you to take. The right answer usually feels modest, even obvious.

parts.title: Part 2 · The four-step method
parts.html:
1. Break the text into bullet points. Give each idea its own line, in order. This lays the argument out step by step and shows where the gap is.
  2. Examine the argument. How do the bullets connect? What do they add up to? Work like a detective: every clue you need is on the page. By the end you should have a rough idea of what belongs in the blank, or at least of what does not.
  3. Go through the choices one at a time. Does this choice complete the argument? Be suspicious of any choice that widens the topic or brings in something the passage never mentioned. These arguments are narrow, and the answer stays inside them.
  4. Pick the choice that strengthens the argument. Read the passage with your choice in the blank. The whole thing should now be clearer and more convincing than before.

parts.title: Part 3 · Worked example: completing the reasons
parts.html:
Adaptations to cold temperatures have high metabolic costs. It is expensive, in terms of energy use, for land plants and animals to withstand very cold temperatures, and it gets more expensive the colder it gets, which means that the lower the air temperature, the fewer species have evolved to survive it. This factor, in conjunction with the decline in air temperature with increasing elevation, explains the distribution of species diversity in mountain ecosystems: you find fewer species high up a mountain than at the mountain’s base because ______ Which choice most logically completes the text?
A) there are relatively few environments hospitable to species that are adapted to live in low air temperatures.
B) there are relatively few species with the adaptations necessary to tolerate the temperatures at high elevations.
C) adaptations that allow plants and animals to survive in rocky environments are metabolically costly.
D) some mountain environments are at elevations so high that no plants or animals can survive them.

Bullet points.

  • Surviving cold costs a lot of energy.
  • So the colder it is, the fewer species have evolved to survive it.
  • Air gets colder as you go up a mountain.
  • There are fewer species near the top than at the base.

Examine the argument. The last bullet is the conclusion, and it is already stated. The blank follows “because”, so it must be the link that joins the first three bullets to the fourth.

Go through the choices.

  • A is about how many environments suit cold-adapted species. The passage is about how many species can stand the cold.
  • C brings in rocky environments, which the passage never mentions.
  • D makes a new claim, that some places have no life at all. It does not explain why there are fewer species higher up.
  • B joins the clues: few species can stand the cold, and it is cold high up, so few species can live high up. B is the answer.

parts.title: Part 4 · Four ways a choice overshoots
parts.html:
• Too strong. The text says the treatment “reduced symptoms in most patients”; the choice says it “cures the condition”. Words like all, always, never, guarantees, proves are red flags. The right answer usually uses calibrated language: may, tends to, often, suggests. When two choices are otherwise equal, the more modest one is more likely correct.
  • Causal leap. The text says two things happen together, or one came first; the choice says one caused the other. This is the most common overshoot in science passages.
  • New information. The choice introduces a fact, group or comparison the text never mentions. It may be true in the real world; it is not an inference from this text.
  • Wrong direction or wrong scope. The text says the policy failed in cities; the choice says it failed in rural areas too. Or the text says results were mixed and the choice says they were uniformly negative.

Common mistake. Treating “not mentioned” as “denied”. If the passage never says the new method works in humans, the inference is not “the method doesn't work in humans”. Absence of evidence is not negative evidence. The safe inference is whatever the text did establish.

parts.title: Part 5 · Tips that save points
parts.html:
TipHow to use it
Stay specificDo not go further than the text allows. A choice can sound relevant to the topic and still be too big a leap, and a small twist in wording can shift what the argument is about.
Watch the strong qualifiersWords that say how much, how many, how often or how likely. Be careful with always and never when the passage describes something that happens sometimes, and with all, most and many when the passage describes one case or a few.
Follow the transitionsContrast words such as however and regardless are especially common here. If two ideas in the passage pull against each other, that tension is usually what the blank has to resolve.
Trust the obvious choiceIf one choice plainly follows from the text, do not talk yourself out of it. The right answer is often the one that feels most directly stated. It is never a stretch.

parts.title: Part 6 · Worked example: a qualification
parts.html:
In a three-year study, volunteers who replaced one hour of daily screen time with walking reported better sleep. The researchers note, however, that participants knew which habit they were practicing. These findings are promising, though ______

Question. Which choice most logically completes the text?

Prediction. “Though” calls for a qualification about the study's reliability, and the “knew which habit” detail was placed there to be used. Something like: the results may partly reflect participants' expectations, not walking itself.

ChoiceVerdict
A) walking is the most effective known intervention for sleep.Too strong. “Most effective known” is supported nowhere.
B) the improvement may be partly due to participants' expectations.Correct. Matches the prediction, uses the planted detail, calibrated language.
C) participants who slept poorly should not walk.New direction. The text makes no recommendations.
D) screen time causes poor sleep in the general population.Causal leap plus scope extension: volunteers are not everyone.

B is the least dramatic choice. That is the pattern: on inference questions, modest wins.

parts.title: Part 7 · What you can and cannot conclude
parts.html:
Look near the blank. The sentence that sets up the conclusion is usually the one just before the blank. Earlier sentences are mostly background. Restate that key sentence in three to six words or as an arrow (“A ↑ → B ↓”) before you read the choices.

A valid inference is the text seen from another angle. It adds nothing. Very often it is the same fact stated from the other side, with a negative.

The text saysYou can conclude
The glue holds best below 10°C.It holds less well in warmer conditions.
The moth flies only at dusk.It does not fly at midday.
About 15% of the island's birds are migrants.Most of the island's birds are not migrants.
Until 2015 the fungus was thought to be rare, because surveys were carried out only in summer.It is more common than was believed, and much of it appears outside summer.

What you cannot conclude.

  • That something is the only way or the best way, when the text says only that it is used or that it works.
  • Anything about a time, place or group the text does not cover. Data “since 2000” says nothing about 1990.
  • Why people did something, when the text reports only what they did.
  • What anyone should do. A text that describes a problem is not recommending a solution.

Translate double negatives first. Two negatives make a positive, and choices use them to disguise a correct answer.

WordingMeans
not uncommonfairly common
not impossiblepossible
hardly insignificantsignificant
cannot be ruled outis possible

Different words are not a new idea. The correct choice almost never repeats the text's wording, so “I did not see that phrase in the text” is not a reason to cross it out. Ask whether the choice rephrases something the text established (valid) or adds something the text never said (invalid). That one distinction settles most hard inference questions.
